statement: Momolu Duwalu Bukele created the Vai syllabary in Liberia, c. 1832-1834. Missionary-recorded founding accounts describe a dream in which a stranger appeared with "a book" and taught him signs he reconstructed on waking with male relatives/friends; near-contemporary transcriptions of this story vary (a Christian missionary's 1834 account vs. Sigismund Koelle's 1849 recording), which scholars read as evidence the "dream" is a status-conferring founding narrative rather than a literal account of a mundane, contact-inspired invention process. Tuchscherer and Hair (History in Africa 29, 2002, pp. 427-486) document that a Cherokee man, Austin Curtis, emigrated to Liberia in 1823 and married into a Vai chief's family, raising the possibility that awareness of the Cherokee syllabary reached Bukele's circle — but Vai characters bear no visual resemblance to Cherokee ones, so any such contact would have transmitted only the concept of syllabic writing, not sign forms. Coded STIMULUS_DIFFUSION on this basis (broader Western/coastal-Liberian literacy exposure, possibly compounded by Cherokee-case awareness).
scholarly_disagreement: The dream narrative is a recorded community tradition with internally inconsistent transcriptions; scholars treat it as likely a religious/status gloss on a documentable contact-inspired process, not a settled literal account either way.

sources.citation: Tuchscherer, Konrad, and P.E.H. Hair. "Cherokee and West Africa: Examining the Origins of the Vai Script." History in Africa 29, 2002: 427-486.
sources.author: Tuchscherer and Hair
